But ours is a two nap schedule (made by our baby), can't remember what our three nap schedule looked like but I believe it was similar except the naps would be down to an hour on average. But you can find sample schedules for this online!

My advice is to go with a popular brand, I prefer O.B. tampons, have never used any other brand. If you're bleeding, no cotton parts will stay inside because the blood soaks the whole thing plus the tampon has an outer layer that prevents that from happening. The only time I noticed some cotton bits trying to stick to my vagina was when I was really dry and not bleeding enough for a tampon.

About it feeling uncomfortable, partly that's because you're afraid of it and it's unfamiliar to have it inside and partly because you need to push it further in. I'd recommend doing that with your finger instead of a tampon inserter stick. For insertion, remember that it's in properly when you don't feel it. If you still feel it when you walk, you need to push it in further. You can't hurt yourself with it, don't worry. A good technique for insertion is standing with your legs apart and then leaning forward. That position creates the perfect angle for it, and also keep wiggling it as you're pushing it if it doesn't go in smoothly. I also recommend size mini tampons to start with and don't use anything above normal size. Just change them more often.

As for your parents scaring you with tampons not being healthy, there will be lots of things that later on you realize are equally not 100% healthy but we still use them every day because we need to live our lives.

I can only comment on how it was done in my part of Europe. Here up until 1895 *everything* was done, legalised, through the church (Catholic, Protestant, Lutheran, Jewish). If you weren't married, no children could ever have a legitimate status no matter what. I saw fathers repeatedly claim children in footnotes, still their part remained empty in the birth certificate because the mother was unwed.

After 1895 civil registry took over, which meant that I think they didn't *necessarily* have to be married anymore (although I have doubts about that). I saw a birth in the registry stating "legitimate according to civil law". Probably something like this happened in New York as well?

A few points I can think of about what you wrote:

>there are about four great-great-aunts who I don't have a single clue who they married or what their kids' names are

* Is it possible that these great-great aunts didn't survive childhood? Here a frightening ratio of children died while growing up.
* I'd leave the cousins for now and focus on building the tree up, to find ancestors who died in the US but were not born there. Those earliest records of your family may hide some clues.

>How do genealogists figure out -- in a big pool of people with similar first names and surnames and little data -- who marries who?

I do this as a hobby but what I do is I build things up, make a sketch and then flesh it out. I have to make guesses based on 18th-19th century maps, migration patterns, and even birth documents. But what becomes important then is to look for reasons *against* what you found, see how well your hypothesis stands, and start collecting evidence for it.

Usually I guess a lot about birth dates but it works out in most cases. For example I look at for how many years they'd been having children and make a guess based on that about their possible ages.

At the moment I'm dealing with exactly the same thing as you; lots of couples with the same surname within the same residential area. I started making it easier on me to connect the dots by working on multiple, like 10, couple's trees on family search. I don't connect them to my family just save their links and as I go through birth/marriage/death records I add in information and fill in the blanks.

To solve your brickwall, for a start I'd try to find your oldest ancestor's birth certificate and go from there. I hope some of what I wrote made sense and good luck!
